column3: The immediate continuation says God inherits the claimed wealth and children and brings the speaker alone before Him.
The wisdom of the Book does not develop the recorded boast or its punishment.
The doomed recipient's regret over his record parallels the focus's warning that speech is entered into account.
God hears an arrogant claim, records it, and answers it with punishment in a near-exact parallel.
Jesus's declaration about birth, death, and resurrection does not illuminate the boast or its record.
Receiving one's book in the right hand provides a judgment-record contrast to the focus's recorded culpable speech.
The same immediate passage says the Most Merciful may extend respite to one in error until the promised punishment is seen.
This is the disbeliever's boast of future wealth and children that 19:79 directly repudiates.
The revelation's source does not clarify the claim, its recording, or extended punishment.
Its emphatic future knowledge faintly echoes the focus's decisive rejection of a false claim.
The warning against disputing without knowledge is too general to develop this specific accountability scene.
It warns against extending one's gaze toward others' worldly enjoyment, qualifying the value of the boast's wealth.
It links divine humiliation to deserved punishment but has no specific relation to the recorded boast.
The true word about Jesus is unrelated to the claimant's statement and resulting penalty.
The earth's being spread out shares only an unrelated verbal form of extension.
God's creative command does not clarify the recording and punishment of the boast.
The immediately preceding challenge asks whether the claimant knows the unseen or possesses a covenant with the Most Merciful.
The deniers' assertion that they will not be punished is a broad parallel to the false security rejected here.
God's general extension of worldly gifts gives limited context for the claimant's presumed future provision.
The same surah declares that God has fully counted everyone, reinforcing the focus's exact recording of speech.
The recurring question about divine punishment supplies only a general punitive resonance.
God's creative command is not a useful neighbor to the judicial recording of a human claim.
Its declaration of a worse recompense and misguidance is only broadly related to the claimant's evil outcome.
The command for upright speech concerns care for heirs, not divine recording of arrogant speech.
The punishment outside the barrier is a general afterlife parallel without the focus's claim-and-record logic.
The false assertion that the Most Merciful has taken a child is another grave saying in the same surah, but a different passage.
Moses's address to Pharaoh does not illuminate this individual boast or its accounting.
Its emphatic rejection of refuge only loosely parallels the focus's opening rejection and future reckoning.
The same surah states that every person comes to God alone, completing the focus passage's reversal of claimed possessions.
Turning from God's reminder leads into a rising punishment, paralleling the focus's extension into punishment.
Denying God's signs and receiving evil punishment is a broad analogue to the focus's unbelieving claimant.
The believers' request to be written among witnesses uses writing affirmatively and does not develop punitive recording.
The extended pillars of Hell share only an unrelated extension image.
The oath formula beginning with no is not a useful neighbor to the focus's rejection and account.
The same surah's false claim about the Most Merciful is thematically related as another condemned saying.
A man boasts to his companion of greater wealth and offspring, closely paralleling the claim rejected in the focus.
A prophet's rejection of being worshiped is not a material link to this boast and punishment.
The same passage tells the Prophet not to hasten the deniers because God is counting out their days.
The rhetorical denial that opponents possess the unseen directly parallels 19:78's challenge to the claimant's assumed knowledge.
Its severe punishment for selective disbelief is a general accountability parallel only.
Hoarded wealth becomes a burden and all inheritance returns to God, complementing the focus's reversal of claimed property.
The companion rebukes an affluent speaker for disbelief in his Creator, directly challenging boastful worldly self-assurance.
Upright scriptures do not clarify the recorded speech or extended punishment.
The same-surah denial of divine sonship concerns a separate false claim and does not develop this scene.
Fear of the Lord's punishment is a general ethical counterpoint to the claimant's false security.
The list of prophets and divine gifts does not illuminate the focus ayah.
David and Solomon's grateful response to knowledge does not clarify the boast's accountability.
The travelers' request for food has no material relation to the focus.
The extended shade shares only an unrelated lexical image.
Jesus's devotion to his mother does not develop the claimant's boast or punishment.
Rescue from painful punishment is broadly relevant but does not clarify why the claimant is punished.
God's provision to a people only distantly relates to the claimant's expectation of future wealth and children.
God records the work of every believing doer, providing a positive counterpart to recording the claimant's words.
Moses's objection to damaging the ship does not illuminate this accountability scene.
God records what people send ahead and their traces, directly supporting the focus's recording of the claimant's statement.
The prescribed punishment for violent corruption is not a close parallel to this individual verbal claim.
Enduring punishment for deeds broadly resembles the focus's punitive consequence.
The destruction of former peoples does not clarify the recorded boast.
Punishment follows what hands have sent ahead, supplying the retributive principle behind recording the claimant's speech.
Invalid argument followed by wrath and severe punishment broadly parallels an arrogant claim's failure.
The grant of abundant wealth forms a contextual counterpoint to the claimant's expected wealth before his punishment in the same portrait.
Solomon's service from devils does not illuminate the focus's judicial record.
Moses's plea over forgetfulness is unrelated to the boast and punishment.
God's book speaks the truth against people because their deeds were being copied, closely paralleling recorded speech as evidence.
The beautification of disbelievers' deeds offers a broad explanation for deluded confidence, without the focus's specific claim.
It distinguishes a worldly punishment from the greater punishment of the Hereafter, reinforcing the warning of extended torment.
The accusation that a messenger is a liar is another false saying, but not a close link to the focus's accounting.
The Book's mission from darkness to light does not clarify the claimant's recorded boast.
The preparation of painful punishment for wrongdoers is a general outcome parallel.
The same surah selects those most insolent toward the Most Merciful for judgment, framing the claimant's insolence.
The rhetorical denial that opponents possess the unseen closely matches the challenge posed in 19:78.
It tells disbelievers they cannot escape God and announces painful punishment, directly countering presumed security.
It questions whether ongoing wealth and sons are mistaken for divine favor, closely exposing the logic behind the boast.
Treaty-breaking and lack of God-consciousness do not clarify this personal claim and its record.
The call to sincere worship and hope in meeting God is a broad corrective to unbelief, not a close neighbor.
God's promise to drive the arrogant wealthy man into arduous punishment parallels the focus's extended punishment.
God's universal dominion and return to Him do not specifically develop the focus.
The instruction to speak kindly in property management is unrelated to divine recording of a boast.
The written decree that Satan's follower reaches Hell is a general written-liability and punishment parallel.
Livestock created for human ownership does not illuminate the claimant's future-property assertion.
It forbids extending one's gaze to others' transient worldly splendor, countering confidence in material possessions.
The tasting of lesser punishment before the greater punishment parallels the focus's announced extension of torment.
The revealed Book containing people's mention does not develop the recorded claim or its penalty.
It warns those who say God has taken a child, paralleling the condemnation of a grave false statement.
Sharing punishment on the Day is a general consequence parallel only.
Solomon's command over the wind does not relate to the focus's claim or punishment.
The painful punishment enveloping people is a broad image of the focus's promised torment.
Its emphatic future knowledge faintly echoes the focus's definitive rejection of false security.
The question about a burdensome fee does not clarify the claimant's boast or recorded words.
A community's threat of painful punishment is not comparable to God's judicial response to the claimant.
The punishment of a wrongdoer before return to God is a broad retributive parallel.
The correction of a man proud of wealth and children directly challenges the material confidence underlying the focus's claim.
The threatened cutting of a messenger's aorta is unrelated to the claimant's recorded boast.
The instruction for gentle speech to those seeking aid does not concern divine recording or punishment.
The drink mixture of the righteous has no material relation to the focus.
God has enumerated everything in a written record, directly reinforcing the focus's promise to record what is said.
The denial that revelation is a soothsayer's speech concerns a different type of saying and record.
The dying person's request to return shows belated regret, broadly compatible with the focus's future accountability.
The subjection of celestial signs does not illuminate the focus's boast or its punishment.
God's knowledge is preserved in a book that neither errs nor forgets, supporting the reliability of the focus's record.
It recalls earlier generations superior in wealth and appearance who were destroyed, directly challenging confidence in possessions.
It contrasts transient worldly display with lasting righteous deeds, qualifying the claimant's material expectation.
The immediate continuation exposes the claimant's turn to false gods in pursuit of honor, extending his deluded security.
The false gods will reject their worship and oppose them, continuing the reversal of the claimant's expected support.
God's release of devils to incite the disbelievers explains the ongoing escalation of their defiant claims.
The gathering of the righteous before the Most Merciful contrasts with the claimant's solitary, punitive end.
The driving of criminals to Hell in thirst supplies the larger destination of the punishment announced in the focus.
Intercession is restricted to one holding a covenant from the Most Merciful, answering the claimant's unsupported assumption of such a covenant.
The surrounding condemnation of a monstrous false statement is related to the surah's judgment of grave sayings, though not the same claim.
Creation's near collapse over the false attribution of a child intensifies the passage's broader condemnation of corrupt speech.
Those who presume only a brief touch of Hell are asked whether they possess a covenant from God, closely paralleling 19:78's challenge.
The extension granted to disbelievers is not good for them but increases sin, directly paralleling extended punishment after false security.
God records what hypocrites plot by night, providing a close parallel to His writing down culpable speech.
Worldly openings lead heedless deniers to sudden seizure, countering the inference that material abundance signals favor.
God gradually draws deniers on from where they do not know, a close counterpart to the focus's extended consequence.
God grants respite while His plan is firm, directly illuminating the temporal extension in the focus.
Wealth and children are made a means of worldly punishment and miserable death for disbelievers, reversing the focus claimant's expectation.
The repeated warning that wealth and children are a means of punishment closely parallels the focus's reversal of the boast.
Every person's deeds are fastened to him and produced in a book on the Day of Resurrection, extending the focus's written liability.
The command to read one's record makes explicit the personal accounting implied by God recording the claimant's words.
The garden owner enters his property wronging himself, introducing the wealthy speaker's self-delusion that parallels the focus.
The garden owner denies the Hour and expects an even better return, closely matching the claimant's presumed prosperous future.
His companion warns that God may destroy the garden, directly overturning the confidence placed in worldly property.
The garden owner's wealth is destroyed and becomes a source of regret, completing the reversal of material boastfulness.
Wealth and children are only the adornment of worldly life, directly qualifying the claimant's boast of both.
The book leaves out neither small nor great deeds, closely supporting the focus's promise to record what is said.
It denies that ongoing wealth and children mean God is hastening good to their possessors, directly completing 23:55's challenge.
Wealth and children will not benefit on the Day of Judgment, directly refuting the claimant's confidence in both.
Only one who comes to God with a sound heart benefits, supplying the corrective to material claims of security.
The two receivers take down a person's deeds, directly supporting the focus's promise to write the claimant's speech.
No utterance is made without a ready watcher, an exact accountability parallel to recording what he says.
God enumerates forgotten deeds and informs people of them, reinforcing the exhaustive record behind the focus's warning.
Believers are warned not to let wealth and children distract from God's remembrance, directly identifying the spiritual danger behind the boast.
Wealth and children are a trial, not a guarantee of favor, directly correcting the claimant's expectation.
God gives respite to those who deny the revelation, closely paralleling the focus's extension of consequence.
The divine reprieve is paired with an irresistible plan, directly clarifying that delay is not acquittal.
Wealth and sons accompany the denier's rejection of revelation in a closely related portrait of privileged arrogance.
The privileged denier dismisses God's signs as tales of the former peoples, a comparable culpable utterance.
The arrogant opponent is granted sons constantly present, directly paralleling the claimant's expectation of children.
God makes circumstances easy for that opponent, forming the worldly provision that he mistakes for security.
Despite abundant provision, he greedily hopes for more, closely matching the boastful expectation overturned in the focus.
His stubborn rejection of God's signs establishes why the subsequent threat of punishment is deserved.
Watchers are set over every person, supporting the focus's assertion that words are written down.
The noble scribes provide the recording agents implicit in the focus's judicial declaration.
Their knowledge of what people do completes the accountability logic of the recorded statement.
Receiving one's record in the right hand provides a positive judgment-book counterpart to the focus's written liability.
Receiving one's record from behind one's back provides the punitive counterpart to the focus's recorded speech.
The hoarder who counts his wealth is a direct portrait of false confidence in accumulated possessions.
He imagines his wealth will make him immortal, closely paralleling the claimant's presumption of an assured future.
The hoarder is cast into the Crusher, supplying the punitive reversal of his material confidence.
Wealth and what one earned do not avail Abu Lahab, directly countering confidence in possessions before punishment.
